questions.q: Which anatomical division of the nervous system comprises the brain and spinal cord?
questions.explain: The central nervous system (CNS) consists of the brain and spinal cord, whereas the peripheral nervous system (PNS) consists of cranial nerves, spinal nerves, peripheral branches, and ganglia outside the CNS.

open.q: Which division of the nervous system consists of the brain and spinal cord?

questions.q: How many pairs of spinal nerves typically emerge from the human spinal cord?
questions.explain: There are 31 pairs of spinal nerves: 8 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral, and 1 coccygeal. There are 12 pairs of cranial nerves.

open.q: How many pairs of spinal nerves are typically present in the human body?

questions.q: Which root of a spinal nerve carries predominantly afferent (sensory) axons into the spinal cord?
questions.explain: The dorsal (posterior) root carries afferent sensory fibers from peripheral receptors into the spinal cord, with cell bodies located in the dorsal root ganglion. The ventral (anterior) root carries efferent motor fibers.

open.q: Which root of a spinal nerve conducts sensory impulses toward the spinal cord?

questions.q: Where are the cell bodies of somatic and visceral afferent neurons of a spinal nerve typically located?
options: Ventral horn of the spinal cord
questions.explain: Pseudounipolar sensory neuron cell bodies reside in the dorsal (posterior) root ganglion along the dorsal root of each spinal nerve. Motor cell bodies for skeletal muscle lie in the ventral horn of the spinal cord.

open.q: Where are the cell bodies of sensory neurons entering a spinal nerve located?

questions.q: Why do thoracic spinal nerves (T2 to T11) generally run independently as intercostal nerves rather than forming limb plexuses?
options: Anterior rami remain segmental to supply the trunk wall
They lack dorsal roots and sensory fibres
They end in the sympathetic trunk
They fuse into one trunk before exiting the vertebral canal
questions.explain: Anterior rami of C5 to T1 form the brachial plexus and L1 to S4 form the lumbar and sacral plexuses for the limbs, whereas most thoracic anterior rami stay segmental as intercostal/subcostal nerves supplying the trunk wall.

open.q: Why do most thoracic spinal nerves remain segmental instead of forming plexuses like cervical, lumbar, and sacral nerves?
accept: their anterior rami supply the segmented thoracic and abdominal walls
anterior rami stay segmental for body wall innervation
they supply segmental intercostal and abdominal wall territories
their anterior rami do not merge into limb plexuses

questions.q: What is a nerve plexus formed by the anterior rami of spinal nerves?
options: Postganglionic sympathetic fibres within an artery wall
A nerve network redistributing fibres from several spinal levels into peripheral nerves
A sheath around a nerve fascicle
A sensory receptor capsule in deep fascia
questions.explain: A somatic nerve plexus (such as the cervical, brachial, lumbar, or sacral plexus) is a network where anterior rami exchange fibers so individual peripheral nerves receive axons from more than one spinal cord segment.

open.q: What is a somatic nerve plexus formed by anterior rami?
accept: an interlacing network of nerves redistributing fibers from multiple spinal segments
a network of nerve fibers combining multiple spinal levels
nerve network redistributing fibers into peripheral nerves

questions.q: From which spinal cord levels do preganglionic sympathetic cell bodies primarily originate in the intermediolateral cell column?
questions.explain: The sympathetic outflow is thoracolumbar, arising from preganglionic sympathetic neurons in the lateral horn (intermediolateral column) of spinal segments T1 through L2 (or L3). Craniosacral outflow provides parasympathetic innervation.

open.q: From which spinal cord segments does the preganglionic sympathetic outflow originate?

questions.q: Which cranial nerve carries the largest share of parasympathetic preganglionic fibers to thoracic and most abdominal viscera?
questions.explain: The vagus nerve (CN X) provides parasympathetic innervation to the heart, airways, and gastrointestinal tract from the esophagus through the midgut/hindgut transition. Sacral parasympathetic fibers (S2 to S4) supply the distal colon and pelvic viscera.

open.q: Which cranial nerve supplies parasympathetic fibers to the heart, lungs, and most of the gastrointestinal tract?

questions.q: Why do postganglionic sympathetic fibers reach sweat glands, arrector pili muscles, and skin blood vessels throughout the body wall and limbs?
options: Gray rami return postganglionic sympathetic fibres to spinal nerves
Parasympathetic ganglia lie inside every sweat gland
Somatic sensory fibres become sympathetic in skin
Sympathetic fibres travel only inside arteries
questions.explain: Postganglionic sympathetic fibers leave sympathetic ganglia via gray rami communicantes to join spinal nerves and travel along their branches to effectors in the body wall and limbs. White rami communicantes carry myelinated preganglionic fibers from T1 to L2 into the sympathetic chain.

open.q: How do postganglionic sympathetic fibers enter spinal nerves to reach effectors in the body wall and limbs?

questions.q: A patient has a lesion involving the cervical sympathetic trunk on the right side and presents with ptosis, miosis, and anhidrosis on the right face. Which syndrome does this triad describe?
questions.explain: Interruption of the oculosympathetic pathway produces Horner syndrome, classically characterized by miosis (constricted pupil), partial ptosis (drooping upper eyelid), and facial anhidrosis (loss of sweating) on the affected side.

open.q: What syndrome is characterized by ipsilateral ptosis, miosis, and facial anhidrosis after sympathetic pathway interruption?

questions.q: Which layer of a blood vessel wall is the innermost lining composed of endothelium and a subendothelial layer?
questions.explain: The tunica intima is the innermost layer of arteries and veins, consisting of simple squamous endothelium and delicate subendothelial connective tissue. The tunica media is the middle smooth muscle/elastic layer, and the tunica adventitia is the outer connective tissue layer.

open.q: What is the innermost endothelial layer of a blood vessel called?

questions.q: How does the tunica media of an elastic (conducting) artery such as the aorta differ from that of a muscular (distributing) artery?
options: A single layer of flattened cells
Elastic lamellae allow stretch and recoil with the pulse
No smooth muscle or connective tissue
questions.explain: Large elastic arteries have abundant elastic lamellae in the tunica media that expand during ventricular systole and recoil in diastole to maintain continuous blood flow and diastolic pressure. Muscular arteries have proportionally more smooth muscle for regulating flow to specific regions.

open.q: What prominent structural feature in the tunica media of elastic arteries helps maintain pressure during diastole?
accept: abundant elastic fibers or sheets that stretch and recoil

questions.q: What are the small blood vessels located in the adventitia and outer media of large blood vessels that nourish the vessel wall itself?
questions.explain: Vasa vasorum (vessels of the vessel) are tiny arteries and veins supplying oxygen and nutrients to the outer walls of large arteries and veins whose thickness exceeds simple diffusion from the lumen.

open.q: What are the small blood vessels that supply the walls of large blood vessels called?

questions.q: Which structural feature is typically present in medium-sized veins of the limbs to assist unidirectional blood flow toward the heart against gravity?
questions.explain: Many medium-sized veins, especially in the limbs, possess folds of tunica intima forming valves (usually bicuspid) that prevent retrograde flow and support venous return during muscle contraction. Arteries generally lack valves except at the aortic and pulmonary roots.

open.q: What structures inside limb veins help prevent backflow of blood away from the heart?

questions.q: Why are veins generally thinner-walled and more distensible than companion arteries of similar caliber?
options: Thin tunica media with less muscle and elastic tissue; lower pressure
Higher systolic pressure than the aorta
questions.explain: Veins operate at lower pressure and have a thinner tunica media with less elastic tissue and smooth muscle than arteries, making them more compliant and able to hold a large proportion of total blood volume.

open.q: Why are veins more compliant and thinner-walled than arteries of comparable size?
accept: they have a thinner tunica media and experience lower pressure
less smooth muscle and elastic tissue in their wall and lower pressure
thinner tunica media with less smooth muscle and elastin
lower intravascular pressure and thinner muscle layer

questions.q: At which microscopic vessels does exchange of gases, nutrients, and metabolic waste occur between blood and interstitial fluid?
questions.explain: Capillaries consist essentially of a single layer of endothelial cells (and basement membrane), providing a thin barrier and vast surface area for diffusion and filtration between blood and tissues.

open.q: Which blood vessels serve as the primary site of nutrient, gas, and waste exchange with tissues?

questions.q: What is an arterial anastomosis?
options: A valve inside a deep limb vein
A direct communication between branches of two or more arteries
A lymphatic trunk emptying into the thoracic duct
A bundle of sympathetic axons along a nerve
questions.explain: An anastomosis is a connection between vessels; an arterial anastomosis links branches of different arteries to provide collateral pathways and equalize pressure around joints or organs. End arteries lack sufficient anastomoses to sustain tissue if occluded.

open.q: What is an arterial anastomosis?
accept: a connection or communication between branches of arteries
communication between two or more arteries

questions.q: Why does occlusion of a true (anatomical) end artery typically result in tissue ischemia or necrosis of the supplied territory?
options: Few collateral arteries exist beyond the obstruction
questions.explain: True end arteries (such as the central artery of the retina) lack adequate collateral anastomoses with neighboring arteries, so blockage cuts off perfusion to their target tissue and can cause infarction or blindness.

open.q: Why does blockage of a true end artery often cause ischemia or necrosis in its supplied tissue?
accept: lack of adequate collateral arterial anastomoses
absence of effective anastomoses with adjacent arteries

questions.q: A patient has gradual narrowing of a major limb artery, yet distal perfusion is partially preserved through smaller vessels bypassing the stenosis around the joint. What are these alternative channels called?
questions.explain: Collateral circulation consists of preexisting or newly recruited anastomotic vessels that bypass an obstructed artery to maintain blood flow to distal tissues. Around joints, rich arterial anastomoses help preserve circulation during limb flexion.

open.q: What term describes alternative anastomotic blood pathways that bypass a narrowed or blocked artery?

questions.q: What is a direct vascular connection between an arteriole and a venule that bypasses the intervening capillary bed?
questions.explain: An arteriovenous anastomosis (AV shunt) links a small artery/arteriole directly to a vein/venule without passing through capillaries, playing roles in thermoregulation (such as in skin of digits) and local blood flow regulation.

open.q: What is a direct vessel connection between an arteriole and a venule that bypasses capillaries?

questions.q: In limbs and body walls, which structures commonly travel together within a common connective tissue sheath as a neurovascular bundle?
questions.explain: A neurovascular bundle typically contains an artery, one or more accompanying veins, and a nerve running together along a protected fascial plane or intermuscular groove. Knowing their arrangement helps surgeons avoid injury during dissection.

open.q: Which three main structures commonly run together in a neurovascular bundle?
accept: an artery, a vein, and a nerve

questions.q: Why are venae comitantes (paired veins flanking a deep artery in the limbs) helpful for venous return?
options: Arterial pulsation and muscle contraction help propel venous blood
They carry arterial blood to digits
They prevent venous valves from closing
questions.explain: Venae comitantes run closely alongside deep arteries (especially in limbs), where arterial pulsations and adjacent skeletal muscle contraction assist venous return past one-way venous valves.

open.q: How do venae comitantes running beside a deep limb artery assist venous return?
accept: arterial pulsations and muscle contraction help pump blood along valved veins
pulsations of the neighboring artery help propel blood
arterial pulsation and skeletal muscle pump assist flow
they benefit from adjacent arterial pulsations and muscle compression

questions.q: Which major lymphatic vessel collects lymph from the lower limbs, abdomen, left thorax, left upper limb, and left side of the head and neck?
questions.explain: The thoracic duct is the largest lymphatic channel in the body, draining lymph from below the diaphragm plus the left half of the thorax, left arm, and left head/neck into the systemic venous system near the left brachiocephalic/internal jugular-subclavian junction.

open.q: Which main lymphatic vessel drains lymph from the lower body and the left side of the upper body into the venous system?

questions.q: Why do lymphatic capillaries have a more permeable endothelial lining and anchoring filaments than typical blood capillaries?
options: They pump red cells at arterial pressure
They return interstitial fluid, proteins and debris to blood
They filter urine before the ureter
questions.explain: Lymphatic capillaries have overlapping endothelial junctions and anchoring filaments that open when interstitial fluid pressure rises, allowing uptake of excess tissue fluid, proteins, and particulate matter to form lymph.

open.q: What functional advantage does the permeable wall of lymphatic capillaries provide?
accept: uptake of interstitial fluid, proteins, and debris
absorption of excess tissue fluid and large proteins
draining interstitial fluid and proteins that cannot enter blood capillaries

questions.q: A patient undergoes axillary lymph node dissection for breast cancer and later develops persistent swelling of the ipsilateral upper limb. Which mechanism accounts for this swelling?
options: Impaired lymph drainage causes protein-rich oedema
questions.explain: Removal or disruption of regional lymph nodes and lymphatic channels impairs clearance of interstitial fluid and proteins, leading to fluid retention in the subcutaneous tissue known as lymphedema.

open.q: What mechanism explains persistent arm swelling after axillary lymph node clearance?
accept: blocked or disrupted lymphatic outflow leading to fluid retention
disrupted lymphatic drainage and interstitial fluid buildup

questions.q: What is the outermost connective tissue sheath surrounding an entire peripheral nerve?
questions.explain: The epineurium is the outermost dense connective tissue sheath binding the fascicles of a peripheral nerve together.

open.q: What is the outermost connective tissue sheath of a peripheral nerve called?

questions.q: Which nerve sheath surrounds a single fascicle and forms the blood-nerve barrier?
questions.explain: The perineurium surrounds each fascicle and its tight junctions form the blood-nerve barrier.

open.q: Which nerve sheath surrounds a single fascicle and forms the blood-nerve barrier?

questions.q: What is the delicate connective tissue surrounding each individual nerve fibre called?
questions.explain: The endoneurium is the delicate connective tissue around individual axons and their Schwann cells.

open.q: What is the connective tissue around a single nerve fibre called?

questions.q: Which type of nerve fibre is most heavily myelinated and conducts fastest?
questions.explain: A-alpha fibres are the largest, most heavily myelinated fibres and conduct at the highest velocity.

open.q: Which nerve fibre type conducts impulses fastest?

questions.q: Which nerve fibre type carries slow, burning pain and is unmyelinated?
questions.explain: C fibres are thin, unmyelinated fibres that conduct slowly and carry dull, burning pain and autonomic signals.

open.q: Which unmyelinated nerve fibres carry slow burning pain?

questions.q: What is the general name for the junction between an autonomic nerve fibre and its effector cell?
questions.explain: A neuroeffector junction is the junction between an autonomic nerve fibre and its effector (smooth muscle, cardiac muscle, or gland).

open.q: What is the general name for the junction between an autonomic nerve and its effector cell?

questions.q: Which cranial nerves are purely sensory?
questions.explain: CN I (olfactory), CN II (optic) and CN VIII (vestibulocochlear) are purely sensory nerves.

open.q: Which cranial nerves are purely sensory?

questions.q: Which neurotransmitter is released by all postganglionic parasympathetic fibres?
questions.explain: Postganglionic parasympathetic fibres release acetylcholine; they are cholinergic.

open.q: Which neurotransmitter do postganglionic parasympathetic fibres release?

questions.q: Which vessels are the main site of peripheral resistance in the circulation?
questions.explain: Arterioles have relatively thick smooth muscle and are the main resistance vessels that regulate blood flow and pressure.

open.q: Which vessels are the main site of peripheral resistance?

questions.q: Which type of capillary is found in endocrine glands and the intestine and has fenestrations?
questions.explain: Fenestrated capillaries have pores that permit rapid exchange of fluids and small molecules, as in endocrine glands and the intestine.

open.q: Which capillary type has pores for rapid exchange?

questions.q: Which type of capillary is found in the liver, spleen and bone marrow and has large gaps between endothelial cells?
questions.explain: Sinusoidal capillaries have large gaps and a discontinuous basal lamina, allowing cells and large molecules to pass.

open.q: Which capillary type has large gaps and is found in liver and spleen?

questions.q: A patient has a laceration in the axilla with loss of sensation over the lateral shoulder and weakness of shoulder abduction. Which nerve is most likely injured?
questions.explain: The axillary nerve supplies the deltoid and the skin over the lateral shoulder; injury causes sensory loss and weak abduction.

open.q: Which nerve supplies the deltoid and skin over the lateral shoulder?

questions.q: What is the clinical term for reduced blood flow to a tissue that can lead to cell death?
questions.explain: Ischaemia is reduced blood flow to a tissue, which can cause hypoxia and cell death if prolonged.

open.q: What is reduced blood flow to a tissue called?

questions.q: Which nerve fibre type carries touch and pressure and is myelinated but slower than A-alpha?
questions.explain: A-beta fibres are large myelinated fibres that carry touch and pressure at moderate velocity.

open.q: Which myelinated nerve fibre type carries touch and pressure?

questions.q: Which nerve fibre type is thinly myelinated and carries fast, sharp pain and temperature?
questions.explain: A-delta fibres are thinly myelinated and carry fast, sharp, well-localized pain and temperature.

open.q: Which nerve fibre type carries fast sharp pain and temperature?

questions.q: Which neurotransmitter is released at the neuromuscular junction to excite skeletal muscle?
questions.explain: Acetylcholine released from the somatic motor nerve terminal binds nicotinic receptors on the motor end plate to excite skeletal muscle.

open.q: Which neurotransmitter is released at the neuromuscular junction?

questions.q: What is the name of the specialized region of the skeletal muscle fibre membrane that receives the nerve terminal?
questions.explain: The motor end plate is the specialized postsynaptic sarcolemma region rich in nicotinic acetylcholine receptors.

open.q: What is the postsynaptic membrane region of a skeletal muscle fibre at the neuromuscular junction called?

questions.q: Which cranial nerve is purely motor and supplies the tongue?
questions.explain: The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) is purely motor and supplies the intrinsic and extrinsic tongue muscles.

open.q: Which cranial nerve is purely motor and supplies the tongue?

questions.q: Which cranial nerve carries both motor fibres to the muscles of mastication and sensory fibres from the face?
questions.explain: The trigeminal nerve (CN V) is mixed: its motor root supplies muscles of mastication, and its sensory root supplies the face.

open.q: Which cranial nerve supplies the muscles of mastication and sensation of the face?

questions.q: What is the main difference between white and gray rami communicantes?
options: White rami carry myelinated preganglionic fibres; gray rami unmyelinated postganglionic fibres
White rami carry venous blood; gray rami arterial blood
White rami occur only below L2; gray only above T1
White rami are sensory; gray rami are motor
questions.explain: White rami communicantes contain myelinated preganglionic sympathetic fibres (T1 to L2), while gray rami communicantes contain unmyelinated postganglionic fibres joining spinal nerves at all levels.

open.q: What type of fibres do white rami communicantes carry compared with gray rami communicantes?
accept: white carry preganglionic myelinated and gray carry postganglionic unmyelinated fibres
white myelinated preganglionic and gray unmyelinated postganglionic

questions.q: What is the difference between paravertebral and prevertebral sympathetic ganglia?
options: Paravertebral ganglia lie beside the vertebral column; prevertebral ganglia lie anterior to the aorta
Paravertebral ganglia are in the brainstem; prevertebral in spinal cord
Paravertebral ganglia are parasympathetic; prevertebral sympathetic
Paravertebral ganglia are sensory; prevertebral motor
questions.explain: Paravertebral ganglia form the sympathetic chain alongside the vertebral column, while prevertebral (preaortic) ganglia lie anterior to the aorta and supply abdominal viscera.

open.q: Where do paravertebral sympathetic ganglia lie compared with prevertebral ganglia?
accept: paravertebral beside the vertebral column and prevertebral anterior to the aorta
paravertebral in the sympathetic chain, prevertebral in front of the aorta
paravertebral alongside vertebrae and prevertebral anterior to aorta

questions.q: Which of these is a parasympathetic ganglion located near the target organ in the head?
questions.explain: The ciliary ganglion is a parasympathetic ganglion supplying the sphincter pupillae and ciliary muscle; the others are sympathetic ganglia.

open.q: Name a parasympathetic ganglion in the head that supplies the eye.

questions.q: Which part of the nervous system forms the intrinsic nerve plexuses of the gastrointestinal tract?
questions.explain: The enteric nervous system consists of the myenteric (Auerbach) and submucosal (Meissner) plexuses that control gastrointestinal motility and secretion.

open.q: Which division of the nervous system forms the intrinsic nerve plexuses of the gut?

questions.q: What is the main function of the tunica adventitia of a blood vessel?
options: Anchoring the vessel to surrounding tissues
questions.explain: The tunica adventitia is the outer connective tissue layer that anchors vessels to surrounding tissues and contains vasa vasorum and nerves.

open.q: What is the main function of the tunica adventitia?

questions.q: What is the main function of muscular (distributing) arteries?
options: Regulating organ blood flow by vasoconstriction and vasodilation
questions.explain: Muscular arteries have a thick tunica media of smooth muscle that regulates blood flow distribution to specific organs and regions.

open.q: What is the main function of muscular arteries?

questions.q: What is the difference between superficial and deep veins of the limbs?
options: Superficial veins are subcutaneous; deep veins accompany arteries
Superficial veins carry arterial blood; deep veins venous blood
Superficial veins run with nerves; deep veins with tendons
questions.explain: Superficial veins lie in the subcutaneous tissue and drain into deep veins, which run alongside major arteries within the deep fascia.

open.q: Where do superficial limb veins lie compared with deep limb veins?
accept: superficial in subcutaneous tissue and deep alongside arteries
superficial under the skin, deep with arteries
superficial in fat and deep within fascia

questions.q: What are perforating veins of the lower limb?
options: Veins connecting superficial and deep venous systems through fascia
questions.explain: Perforating veins pierce the deep fascia to connect superficial veins with deep veins, with valves normally directing blood inward.

open.q: What do perforating veins of the lower limb connect?

questions.q: What is the portal venous system?
options: Blood passes through two capillary beds in series before returning to heart
questions.explain: In a portal system, blood flows through two capillary beds in series; the hepatic portal vein carries blood from gut capillaries to liver sinusoids before reaching the systemic circulation.

open.q: What defines a portal venous system?
accept: blood passes through two capillary beds

questions.q: What is the cisterna chyli?
options: Dilated sac at the thoracic duct origin receiving intestinal and lumbar lymph
questions.explain: The cisterna chyli is a dilated sac at the lower end of the thoracic duct that receives lymph from the intestinal and lumbar trunks.

open.q: What is the dilated sac at the lower end of the thoracic duct called?

questions.q: Which body regions drain into the right lymphatic duct?
options: Right head and neck, right arm and right thorax
questions.explain: The right lymphatic duct drains the right side of the head and neck, the right upper limb, and the right thorax, emptying into the right venous angle.

open.q: Which regions of the body drain into the right lymphatic duct?
accept: right head and neck, right arm and right thorax
right side of head, neck, thorax and right upper limb

questions.q: What is the function of baroreceptors in the carotid sinus and aortic arch?
options: Detecting arterial pressure changes and initiating reflex responses
questions.explain: Baroreceptors in the carotid sinus and aortic arch detect stretch from blood pressure changes and trigger reflexes to adjust heart rate and vessel tone.

open.q: What do baroreceptors in the carotid sinus and aortic arch detect?

questions.q: What is the function of chemoreceptors in the carotid and aortic bodies?
options: Detecting blood O2, CO2 and pH
questions.explain: Chemoreceptors in the carotid and aortic bodies detect changes in arterial oxygen, carbon dioxide and pH and stimulate respiratory and cardiovascular responses.

open.q: What do chemoreceptors in the carotid and aortic bodies detect?

questions.q: What is the main function of arteriovenous anastomoses in the skin of the digits?
options: Thermoregulation by diverting blood away from skin surface
questions.explain: Arteriovenous anastomoses in the skin of digits shunt blood directly from arterioles to venules, helping regulate body temperature by controlling heat loss.

open.q: What is the main function of arteriovenous anastomoses in the skin?

questions.q: Why do nerves and vessels often run together in neurovascular bundles in the limbs?
options: They follow the same fascial planes and are protected together during movement
They share the same embryonic origin from the neural crest
Nerves produce the blood vessels they supply
Vessels conduct nerve impulses along their walls
questions.explain: Nerves and vessels follow common fascial planes and intermuscular septa, where they are protected from compression during limb movement.

open.q: Why do nerves and vessels travel together in neurovascular bundles in the limbs?
accept: they follow the same fascial planes and are protected together
shared fascial pathways protect them during movement

questions.q: A patient has swelling, pain and pulselessness of the anterior leg after a tibial fracture. Which condition is most likely?
questions.explain: Compartment syndrome occurs when increased pressure within a fascial compartment compromises blood flow, causing pain, swelling and eventually pulselessness and nerve damage.

open.q: Which condition results from increased pressure within a closed fascial compartment compromising blood flow?

questions.q: What is the term for abnormally dilated, tortuous superficial veins, most commonly in the lower limb?
questions.explain: Varicose veins are abnormally dilated and tortuous superficial veins, usually due to incompetent valves and increased venous pressure.

open.q: What is the term for abnormally dilated and tortuous superficial veins?

questions.q: What is the underlying cause of primary varicose veins?
options: Incompetent venous valves cause venous hypertension
questions.explain: Primary varicose veins result from incompetent valves in superficial or perforating veins, causing blood pooling and venous hypertension.

open.q: What is the usual underlying cause of primary varicose veins?

questions.q: What is arteriosclerosis?
options: General thickening and hardening of arterial walls
questions.explain: Arteriosclerosis is a general term for thickening, hardening and loss of elasticity of arterial walls.

open.q: What does the term arteriosclerosis mean?
accept: thickening and hardening of arterial walls

questions.q: What is atherosclerosis?
options: Lipid-rich plaques form in the intima of medium and large arteries
Calcium hardens only the tunica media
questions.explain: Atherosclerosis is a specific form of arteriosclerosis involving intimal plaques containing lipid, smooth muscle, collagen and inflammatory cells in large and medium arteries.

open.q: What is the formation of lipid-rich plaques in the intima of large and medium arteries called?

questions.q: A patient has an atherosclerotic plaque in the left internal carotid artery causing transient right-sided weakness. Which process is most directly responsible for the symptoms?
options: Plaque thrombosis or embolism reduces cerebral blood flow
questions.explain: Atherosclerotic plaque in the carotid can rupture, causing thrombosis or embolism that obstructs cerebral blood flow, leading to transient or permanent neurological deficits.

open.q: Which arterial pathology most directly causes transient ischaemic attacks from carotid artery disease?

questions.q: What is an aneurysm?
options: A persistent local dilation of a vessel wall
questions.explain: An aneurysm is a permanent abnormal dilation of a blood vessel wall, often due to weakness of the tunica media, and can rupture.

open.q: What is a permanent localized dilation of a blood vessel called?

questions.q: What are vasa vasorum?
options: Small vessels supplying the walls of larger vessels
questions.explain: Vasa vasorum are small arteries, veins and capillaries that supply the outer walls of large vessels too thick to be nourished by diffusion from the lumen.

open.q: What are the small vessels supplying the walls of large blood vessels called?

questions.q: Why do large arteries such as the aorta require vasa vasorum?
options: Their thick walls prevent diffusion from the lumen to outer layers
questions.explain: The walls of large arteries are too thick for diffusion from the lumen to nourish the outer media and adventitia, so vasa vasorum supply these layers.

open.q: Why do large arteries need vasa vasorum to supply their walls?
accept: walls too thick for diffusion from lumen
outer layers too far from lumen for diffusion

questions.q: Which type of arteriosclerosis specifically affects small arteries and arterioles, commonly in hypertension and diabetes?
questions.explain: Arteriolosclerosis is thickening and loss of elasticity of small arteries and arterioles, typically seen in hypertension and diabetes.

open.q: What is the term for arteriosclerosis affecting small arteries and arterioles?

questions.q: What is Monckeberg medial calcific sclerosis?
options: Calcification of arterial media without lumen narrowing
questions.explain: Monckeberg sclerosis is calcification of the tunica media of muscular arteries, usually without significant lumen narrowing or symptoms.

open.q: What is calcification of the tunica media of muscular arteries called?

questions.q: Which layer of the artery is primarily affected by atherosclerosis?
questions.explain: Atherosclerosis is an intimal disease, with lipid-rich plaques forming within the tunica intima.

open.q: Which arterial layer is primarily affected by atherosclerosis?

questions.q: A patient with long-standing hypertension develops a dissecting aneurysm of the aorta. Which layer is split in this condition?
questions.explain: A dissecting aneurysm involves a tear in the intima with blood entering and splitting the tunica media, creating a false lumen.

open.q: Which layer of the aortic wall is split in a dissecting aneurysm?

questions.q: What is thrombophlebitis?
options: Inflammation of a vein with thrombus formation
questions.explain: Thrombophlebitis is inflammation of a vein, often with an associated thrombus, commonly in superficial leg veins.

open.q: What is inflammation of a vein with thrombus formation called?

questions.q: What is a deep vein thrombosis (DVT) and why is it dangerous?
options: A deep-vein clot that may embolise to the lungs
A superficial clot that never embolises
A clot in the thoracic duct
questions.explain: DVT is a thrombus in a deep vein, usually of the leg, which can dislodge and travel to the pulmonary arteries as a pulmonary embolism.

open.q: What is the major danger of a deep vein thrombosis?

questions.q: Which of Virchow's triad factors contribute to thrombosis?
options: Endothelial injury, abnormal blood flow and hypercoagulability
questions.explain: Virchow's triad comprises endothelial injury, abnormal (stasis or turbulent) blood flow and hypercoagulability, all predisposing to thrombosis.

open.q: What three factors make up Virchow's triad for thrombosis?
accept: endothelial injury, abnormal flow and hypercoagulability

questions.q: What is an embolus?
options: A travelling intravascular mass that lodges in a distant vessel
A clot fixed at its origin
questions.explain: An embolus is a detached mass (thrombus, fat, air, etc.) traveling in the bloodstream that lodges in a vessel and obstructs flow.

open.q: What is a detached intravascular mass that travels and blocks a distant vessel called?

questions.q: A patient with atrial fibrillation develops sudden occlusion of the middle cerebral artery. What is the most likely source of the embolus?
options: Mural thrombus in the left atrium or appendage
questions.explain: Atrial fibrillation predisposes to stasis and mural thrombus formation in the left atrium or its appendage, which can embolize to the cerebral circulation.

open.q: In atrial fibrillation, which chamber commonly forms the thrombus that embolizes to the brain?

questions.q: What is the consequence of valve incompetence in the perforating veins of the lower limb?
options: Deep-to-superficial reflux causes venous hypertension and varicosities
Lymph fails to drain from the leg
questions.explain: When perforating vein valves fail, blood passes from deep to superficial veins during muscle contraction, raising superficial venous pressure and causing varicosities and skin changes.

open.q: What happens when perforating vein valves become incompetent in the leg?
accept: blood flows from deep to superficial veins causing varicosities

questions.q: A spinal nerve is examined immediately after the dorsal and ventral roots unite, but before it divides into its primary rami. Which description best characterizes this nerve?
options: Mixed, carrying sensory and motor fibres
questions.explain: The dorsal root carries sensory afferents and the ventral root carries motor efferents. Their union forms a short mixed spinal nerve containing both sensory and motor fibres before it divides into dorsal and ventral primary rami.

open.q: What is the functional composition of a typical spinal nerve after the dorsal and ventral roots unite?

questions.q: A penetrating injury damages the posterior primary ramus of a lumbar spinal nerve. Which structure is most directly at risk?
options: Intrinsic back muscles and overlying skin
Lower-limb muscles supplied by the lumbosacral plexus
Viscera of the pelvic cavity only
questions.explain: Posterior (dorsal) primary rami supply the intrinsic deep back muscles and the skin of the posterior trunk. The anterior (ventral) rami supply the anterolateral trunk and form the major limb plexuses.

open.q: Which muscles and skin territory are supplied by posterior primary rami of spinal nerves?
accept: intrinsic back muscles and posterior trunk skin
deep back muscles and overlying skin
